w: A sheer sea cliff on Madeira's south coast, among the highest in Europe, drawing up to 1,800 visitors a day to its lookout platform. It doubles as a trailhead, the usual starting point for hikers heading along the coastal paths above Camara de Lobos.
s: One of Europe's highest sea cliffs, and a trailhead

w: Completed in the late 15th century, this cathedral is among the very few structures on Madeira to survive virtually intact from the island's early colonization. Dedicated to Our Lady of the Assumption, it remains the seat of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Funchal, covering the whole autonomous region.
s: Funchal's cathedral, intact since early colonization
_facts: Seat of the Diocese of Funchal
One of the oldest intact colonial-era structures on Madeira

w: The easternmost point of Madeira, a wind-scoured headland of pyroclastic rock and basalt dykes dating back roughly 100,000 years. Protected as a nature reserve since 1982, it shelters endemic plants and the endangered Mediterranean monk seal. An hour-long path crosses the headland from its entrance to the tip.
_facts: Geology dates to the Late Pleistocene
Habitat for the endangered monk seal Monachus monachus

w: Opened to the public in 1960 on land that once belonged to the family of William Reid, the Scottish founder of Funchal's famous Reid's Hotel. The garden sits above the city, tracing a lineage from private colonial-era estate to public showcase of Madeira's exotic flora.
s: A colonial estate turned public botanical showcase
_facts: Former estate of William Reid, founder of Reid's Hotel

w: A shrine to Cristiano Ronaldo's trophies in Funchal, the footballer's birthplace, built beneath a hotel he developed with the Pestana Group. The floor is laid in traditional Portuguese pavement style, and a bronze Ronaldo statue by Madeiran sculptor Ricardo Velosa stands out front.
s: Cristiano Ronaldo's trophy museum in his hometown
_facts: Hotel built above the museum with the Pestana Group
Bronze statue by Ricardo Velosa out front

w: Madeira's second-highest peak at 1,853m, sitting midway along the high trail between Pico Ruivo and Pico do Arieiro. It has no separate access of its own, reachable only by walking the ridge path connecting the island's two most famous summits.
s: Madeira's second-highest peak, reachable only by trail
_facts: Only accessible via the Pico Ruivo-Pico do Arieiro trail

w: Built in the early 17th century to defend Funchal against pirates and foreign invasion, this fort still commands the harbour from Funchal's old town, the Zona Velha. Its bright yellow walls stand out against the surrounding architecture, and it remains both a cultural landmark and a viewpoint over the Atlantic.
s: A 17th-century fort with unmistakable yellow walls
_facts: Located in Funchal's Zona Velha old town

w: Built in 1922 atop the rocky escarpment of Ponta Vigia on Madeira's western tip, this lighthouse has a focal height of 312 metres, among the highest of any lighthouse on the island. It draws real crowds for a working navigational light: over 15,000 visitors came through in 2018 alone.
s: A clifftop lighthouse 312 metres above the sea

n: Farol da Ponta de São Lourenço
w: The oldest lighthouse on Madeira, built in 1870 atop a small extinct volcano marking the island's extreme eastern tip. Its focal point sits 103 metres above the sea, a modest height that belies its age and its place at the start of the Ponta de Sao Lourenco hiking trail.
s: Madeira's oldest lighthouse, on an extinct volcano
_facts: Sits atop a small extinct volcano

w: Built from 1492 to house daughters of Madeira's nobility, this convent of Poor Clares grew out of a family tomb church ordered by Joao Goncalves Zarco, the island's discoverer, and completed under his son. It functioned until the 19th-century dissolution of Portugal's monasteries, and today houses a kindergarten.
s: A noblewomen's convent built by the discoverer's family
_facts: Founded around a church built for Joao Goncalves Zarco's family tomb
Ceased operating after 19th-century dissolution of monasteries

w: A marine reserve off Funchal Bay protected since 1986, popular with snorkellers and scuba divers who share the water with dusky groupers, moray eels and garden eels. Hunting and fishing are banned throughout Madeira's marine reserves, of which Garajau was the first; Rocha do Navio on the north coast followed.
_facts: Home to dusky groupers and moray eels
First of Madeira's two marine nature reserves

w: The main trailhead for Pico Ruivo, Madeira's highest peak, via the PR1.2 path, marked by a basalt formation locals call the 'standing man'. Three parishes meet here, and since 2002 the University of Madeira's Astronomy Group has held its AstroFesta on this plateau, among the region's best stargazing spots.
s: Trailhead to Pico Ruivo, and a stargazing hotspot
_facts: Main access point to Pico Ruivo via trail PR1.2
Basalt formation known as the 'standing man'
